headline: Great South Bay heats into June rhythm as inlet bass shift from bait to plastics
subhead: With offshore buoys dark and analyst data thin, the estuary's thermal lead over the ocean is doing the heavy lifting on the Fire Island beat.
body_markdown:
The honest opening today is that the data desk is half-blind. The Dr. Fish analyst run came back with no live buoy readings to publish — 44025 south of Fire Island is missing wind, the offshore trio at 44017, 44039 and 44040 are offline, and the regional SST package hasn't refreshed since June 8. So I'm not going to invent a number for you. What I can tell you from the water, the calendar, and the last published satellite pass is that the inside-versus-outside thermal split that defines this beat in early June is now fully established. The bay is running well ahead of the ocean, the inlet is acting as the mixing valve between the two, and every tide cycle is pumping warmer, bait-rich estuary water out over the bar on the drop and dragging cool, cleaner ocean water back in on the flood. That is the engine driving everything from Democrat Point east to the Robert Moses bridges right now.

What that means for the beat is straightforward. The structure that's firing is the structure that sits in the temperature gradient: the inlet throat, the rips off Democrat Point, the bridge abutments at Robert Moses, and the deeper holes just inside Captree. Striped bass are stacking on the outgoing because that's when the warm bay water — loaded with spearing, juvenile bunker, and the first squid pushes — gets fired out into cooler ocean. Fluke have set up on the ocean side of the inlet and along the channel edges where that thermal seam concentrates bait. The slot-and-over class of bass is the dominant grade right now, with a heavy mix of shorts; the truly big migratory fish are mostly north of us, but enough resident and lingering fish remain in the inlet system to make every outgoing tide worth fishing.

The most telling signal in the last few weeks has been the gear shift. Through April and into early May the bay bite was a clam-and-anchor game — bellies on a fishfinder rig, sit on a piece, wait it out. That pattern has clearly broken. The bait in the system has changed, the water has warmed past the threshold where bass want to chase, and the productive boats out of Captree have moved decisively to soft plastics worked through the channel edges and around the bridges. Bass Assassins, paddle-tails on half-ounce to one-ounce heads, slow-rolled or hopped through the current seams on the dropping tide — that's the program. Numbers of fish per trip have gone up and the average size has held, with a healthy ratio of slot and over-slot fish to the inevitable pile of shorts.

On the fluke side, the King Cod and the Captree fleet have been grinding ocean drifts since opening day with real keeper ratios, and that ocean-side bite generally tightens up through June as the bay warms and pushes fish to thermoregulate along the cooler edge outside the inlet. Inside the bay, the back-channel fluke bite is just getting honest — bucktails tipped with Gulp, drifted across the mud-to-sand transitions north of Captree and east toward Patchogue, will start producing better fish as the bay locks into the high sixties. Bluefish are around in patchy fashion, mostly choppers harassing bunker schools when they push into the inlet, and weakfish — always a quiet possibility on this beat in June — are worth a few casts with small plastics on the deeper bay edges at dawn.

Looking three to five days out, the variables I'm watching are wind direction and the next satellite SST refresh. A sustained south or southwest breeze will hold warm surface water against the south side of Fire Island and accelerate the inlet bite; a hard east wind will stack water on the beach, dirty the surf, and push the bay program deeper. The moon is moving toward a stronger tide cycle, which means harder current through the inlet and the bridges — that favors the plastics game and concentrates fish on the down-current sides of structure. If the offshore buoys come back online and we get a clean SST chart, I'll have actual numbers for you next report. Until then, the read is mechanical: fish the outgoing, fish the seams, and let the thermal gradient do the work.

I'd be at the Robert Moses bridges on the first half of the outgoing before sunrise, with a box of paddle-tails and one rod rigged for fluke on the way back through Captree. That's where the water is telling the story right now.
